newsitem.title: CHINA: Red chips - China's dynamic source of funds.
newsitem.headline: Red chips - China's dynamic source of funds.

text.p: China's ambitious drive toward modernisation will require the funnelling of vast amounts of capital into key areas in coming years, and its dynamic red chips are destined to be an important channel.
These China-backed companies, based and listed in Hong Kong, are the darlings of the Hong Kong stock market and raised more than $3 billion during the first half of 1997.
"Equity funding is a relatively new feature for attracting foreign capital into China," said Benny Chiu, research manager at Hongkong Bank.

"The most important way of attracting foreign capital into China is still through foreign loans and foreign direct investment, but this new means of raising funds through the equity markets is developing fast," he added.

Hong Kong boasts the seventh largest stock market in the world and is more attractive than Chinese domestic markets for raising funds. "The issue is that you are gaining access to a much deeper and much more international capital market," said Abhijit Chakraborrti, senior strategist at Lehman Brothers.
With huge financing needs on the mainland, particularly in the infrastructure sector, analysts said China's domestic markets would be unable to satisfy the demand for capital.

Meanwhile, actual foreign investment in China is expected to slip to around $40 billion this year from a record $42.35 billion in 1996, and then hover at around $30 billion a year between 1998 and 2000, according to Chinese economists.

Johnson Cheung, an analyst at Goldman Sachs, said red chips and H-shares -- shares of China-incorporated companies listed in Hong Kong -- raised $4 billion in the first half of 1997, equivalent to about 10 percent of foreign direct investment.
"The ratio could go up to 20 percent," he said.

Cheung said most of the capital raised by red-chip companies was destined for investments in China and red chips were effective users of cash, since listings in Hong Kong enhanced transparency and made them accountable to minority shareholders.
"If you raise money through the equity market, you have to prepare the companies so that they are ready to absorb this sort of capital. You have to do a lot of restructuring," added Chiu.
More flexible than China's lumbering H-share companies, red chips were more effective in adjusting to the changing economic environment, said Cheung.

"Currently most red chips are focusing on infrastructure, particularly toll roads, because of investors' demand for projects with strong cash flow, but this also fits in with the government's needs for more infrastructure investment," he said.

China has said it needs $65 billion for highway construction over the next five years. Chinese highway operators have carried out initial public offerings in Hong Kong and red chips have raised money through share issues.
Shanghai Industrial Holdings, the investment arm of the Shanghai municipal government, raised $619.6 million through a share issue in April to buy two roads in Shanghai.
China Merchants Holdings (International) Co. Ltd. also raised $475 million in April to fund the purchase of toll road and container businesses.
The development of Chinese ports is also a priority, with China hoping to develop trade with increased shipping activity.

Red chip COSCO Pacific Ltd, indirectly controlled by China Ocean Shipping (Group) Co., has been a favoured vehicle and raised $154.9 million in a share placement in March to fund port acquisitions and the expansion of Chinese terminals and container manufacturing plants.
"Basically, what China is doing is modernising," said Howard Gorges, vice chairman at South China Holdings.

China is also due to raise funds for its airline industry in the second half of 1997 with the Hong Kong listings of China Southern Airlines and China National Aviation Corp., an airline company controlled by China's Civil Aviation Administration.

The first listing of a major China-backed telecommunications operator is expected by the end of the year, with the $6 billion initial public offering of China Telecom, a company backed by China's Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications.
